{"id": "14:1/q25", "question": "Why are 'the Mighty' and 'the Praiseworthy' chosen and ordered?", "turns_on": "Whether the order follows the verse's two acts, the traveler's encouragement, or a conceptual order among attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q25/p1", "position": "Might suits revelation and overcoming opponents; praise suits the gift of guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Alusi map the two names to the preceding acts in that order; Ibn Ashur says the unconquerable God's Book proves His purpose and overcomes opponents. Tabatabai says the names call people to accept His blessing and fear punishment; Islahi says only He merits fear and hope."}, {"id": "14:1/q25/p2", "position": "The paired names assure and encourage the path's traveler.", "reasons": "Baydawi says the traveler will not be humiliated or disappointed; Elmalili says refuge in God brings honor by might and bounty; Alusi notes the difficult path and praise of those who walk it."}, {"id": "14:1/q25/p3", "position": "Power is mentioned first because knowledge of power precedes knowledge of divine knowledge and independence.", "reasons": "Alusi reports Razi's explanation but questions his sense of hamid and his ordering argument."}, {"id": "14:1/q25/p4", "position": "Priority may go to negative attributes, like purification before adornment.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this suggestion with 42:11."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q26", "question": "How is 'the Praiseworthy' inflected with 'the Mighty'?", "turns_on": "Whether the second epithet continues the genitive adjective chain or opens an independent clause.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q26/p1", "position": "Al-Hamid is genitive as a second adjective of al-Aziz's referent.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Jishumi state this; Qurtubi compares multiple adjectives without a conjunction, as in 'Zayd the wise, the noble.'"}, {"id": "14:1/q26/p2", "position": "It can be nominative as a new subject with Allah its predicate.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Jishumi allow this alongside the genitive parse; Zajjaj notes further subject-predicate inflections."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q27", "question": "How is the following divine name 'Allah' read and parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the divine name continues the genitive construction across the verse boundary or starts a nominative sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q27/p1", "position": "Allah is nominative, opening a new clause or predicating an omitted 'he'.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid names Nafi and Ibn Amir; Jishumi and Ibn Ashur add Abu Jafar. Thalabi calls them Medinan and Syrian readers and says the following alladhi is predicate; Ibn Ashur says Allah predicates an omitted 'he' and cites al-Sakkaki and poetry by Ibrahim al-Suli for ellipsis. Kashshaf gives 'He is God'; Yaqub raises it on pause."}, {"id": "14:1/q27/p2", "position": "Allah is genitive, appositional to the preceding epithet or linked as an adjective.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid assigns this to Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Asim, Hamza and Kisai; Farisi also notes Hafs agreeing with Abu Amr and a rare al-Asma'i report from Nafi. Ibn Khalawayh and Wahidi distinguish apposition from adjective because Allah became a proper name; Wahidi invokes al-Nabigha's name in poetry. Abu Amr explains fronting as 'path of God, the Mighty, Praiseworthy.' Yaqub uses this in continuous reading."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q28", "question": "Where is the stop after 'the Praiseworthy'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q28/p1", "position": "It is complete with nominative Allah and merely good or adequate with genitive Allah.", "reasons": "Itqan says complete versus good; Nashr notes that a stop's status changes with the reading, comparing another case in wa-ttakhidhu. Ibn Khalawayh and Thalabi connect nominative with a new sentence or Yaqub's pause. Ibn Ashur says both readings identify Allah, with nominative more emphatic."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q29", "question": "How is ṣirāṭ pronounced?", "turns_on": "Which transmitted phonetic realization of the first consonant is followed.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q29/p1", "position": "Some pronounce its ṣād as sīn.", "reasons": "Qiraat-Er links this pronunciation to a possible Syriac strata etymology without changing the meaning."}, {"id": "14:1/q29/p2", "position": "A canonical ishmām gives ṣād a slight zāy quality.", "reasons": "Qiraat-Er describes a midpoint between ṣād and sīn."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q30", "question": "How are the opening letters paused or pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q30/p1", "position": "Each letter is pronounced separately and paused with sukūn.", "reasons": "Qiraat-Er describes the waqf reading's distinct units; Majaz says they are unvoweled names."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q31", "question": "Where and when was the sura revealed, and how many verses has it?", "turns_on": "Whether the Badr-related passage is a Medinan exception to an otherwise Meccan sura.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q31/p1", "position": "It is Meccan, with two verses, 14:28–29, excepted as Medinan.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Ibn Abbas report the exception; Durr and Tabatabai connect those verses to slain Badr polytheists. Abu Hayyan reports Ibn Abbas and Qatada. Study Quran says this is a commonly reported exception."}, {"id": "14:1/q31/p2", "position": "The whole sura is Meccan.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls this the majority view; Ibn Abbas and al-Zubayr report Meccan revelation. Asad places it among late Meccan revelations immediately after sura 71. Razi warns the Meccan/Medinan classification rests on solitary reports and matters chiefly for possible abrogation."}, {"id": "14:1/q31/p3", "position": "The sura has fifty-two verses.", "reasons": "Razi, Baydawi, Biqai and Durr give this count."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q32", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported for this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q32/p1", "position": "The verse concerns opposing responses to Jesus and then Muhammad.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas via Miqsam says former rejecters of Jesus believed Muhammad while former believers in Jesus rejected him; Mawardi and Qurtubi preserve the report."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q33", "question": "How does the opening link to nearby suras and verses?", "turns_on": "Which neighbouring textual pattern is being used to explain the opening.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q33/p1", "position": "It continues al-Ra'd's account of the Book and guidance.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan cites 13:31, 13:37 and 13:43 on Quran, Arabic judgment and a witness with knowledge of the Book; after 13:27's request for a sign, this Book suffices as a sign. Biqai links the closing witness of 13:43 to the Quran's eloquence and knowledge. Islahi says 13:41's indirect warning and promise become explicit here."}, {"id": "14:1/q33/p2", "position": "The repeated language of bringing people from darkness to light connects prophetic missions.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim compares Muhammad and Moses at 14:5; Study Quran cites 14:5, 65:11 and passages where God is subject (2:257, 5:16, 33:43, 57:9). Asad says revelation comes in each people's language, with Quran addressed to all humanity."}, {"id": "14:1/q33/p3", "position": "The opening and conclusion frame one argument about God's oneness and universal warning.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says 14:52 closes the opening's claim, and heaven and earth show all blessing is God's; Ibn Ashur says the path of the owner of all things rebukes idolatrous paths and leads into threatened punishment."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q34", "question": "What is the sura's governing purpose and argument?", "turns_on": "Whether the thematic focus is monotheism and gratitude, Quraysh's warning, or revelation's proof and reach.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q34/p1", "position": "It presents the Quran as the Prophet's enduring sign and universal guide.", "reasons": "Burhan stresses the continuing miracle and the study of inimitability; Tabatabai names it the sign of mission; Asad contrasts former scriptures' local addressees with this universal Quran. Elmalili anticipates an objection to a universal messenger receiving an Arabic Book; Biqai says Arabic clarity and proof make the path unmistakable."}, {"id": "14:1/q34/p2", "position": "It affirms God's oneness and shows revelation guiding people to His path.", "reasons": "Biqai calls Abraham's story its clearest evidence and links the Book to Abraham's prayer for a descendant messenger in 2:129. Tabatabai adds divine lordship, might and praiseworthiness, urging fear, thanks, trust and reflection. Study Quran stresses gratitude versus ingratitude across 14:5, 7, 8, 28, 32–34, 37."}, {"id": "14:1/q34/p3", "position": "It warns Quraysh and promises the believers victory.", "reasons": "Islahi compares the false message to a rootless foul tree, Islam to a lasting tree, and Moses' and Abraham's stories to Quraysh's history and future. Abraham's migration and prayer for Arabia reinforce the argument."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q35", "question": "What does the opening report about the revelation itself?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q35/p1", "position": "It is a special covenant recounting earlier peoples' destruction and Muhammad's community's salvation.", "reasons": "Sulami reports Ja'far's inward account."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q36", "question": "What does 'the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy' imply for idolatry?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q36/p1", "position": "Only the all-owning God's path reaches its destination; idolaters' alternatives fail.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the next relative clause magnifies the known owner of heaven and earth and rebukes deficient idols; the discourse then threatens associators. {"id": "14:1/q38", "question": "What dispute over human acts does the guidance clause raise?", "turns_on": "Whether the guidance effect requires created divine causation or human choice and reasoning.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q38/p1", "position": "God creates and governs guidance, while people acquire acts and the Messenger calls.", "reasons": "Tabari presents this affirmationist account against the Qadariyya. Abu Hayyan sees a Mu'tazilite implication in Zamakhshari's enabling gloss; Alusi reports both Sunni and Mu'tazilite use of the verse."}, {"id": "14:1/q38/p2", "position": "The verse presupposes people's ability to reason and choose faith.", "reasons": "Jishumi argues that if God created belief and unbelief, scripture and the Messenger could not bring a person out of unbelief. Al-Qadi argues the same and says reading the Book leads people to infer God's knowledge, power and wisdom, recognize its miracle and the Messenger's truth, then freely accept its laws. Alusi reports the two schools' competing use of the verse."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q39", "question": "How many metaphors does the enabling interpretation create?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q39/p1", "position": "Three: permission, darkness, and light.", "reasons": "Alusi counts the permission-as-enabling image alongside the paired darkness and light images."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q40", "question": "How do the epithets identify God at the verse boundary?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q40/p1", "position": "They function almost like a proper name for the uniquely worship-worthy God.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari says the next description of those who fear God and obey His command clarifies whom the epithets denote."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q41", "question": "What does the basmala frame at the sura opening?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q41/p1", "position": "It frames the clear Book as mercy from the uniquely perfect God.", "reasons": "Biqai distinguishes God's mercy to all creation through the Book from special grace to chosen servants."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q42", "question": "What adjacent lexical gloss accompanies these notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q42/p1", "position": "Istiḥbāb means seeking to gain love.", "reasons": "Tabrisi distinguishes love as willing benefit or as inclination, desire and appetite, and says bughya and ibtighāʾ mean seeking."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q01", "question": "What is the drink that the condemned gulps?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣadīd is specified simply as wound pus or by the reported origin of the blood and pus.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q01/p1", "position": "It is the foul pus drink, ṣadīd.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls ṣadīd liquid pus from a wound; the drink is repeatedly described as bitter, hot, foul, or repulsive."}, {"id": "14:17/q01/p2", "position": "It is blood and pus from the private parts of prostitutes in the Fire.", "reasons": "Al-Ṣādiq gives this identification in the report preserved by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q02", "question": "What does يتجرعه convey about drinking?", "turns_on": "The force of the derived verbal form: exertion and gradual sipping, equivalence to the simple verb, or response to being made to gulp.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q02/p1", "position": "He reluctantly forces down the drink in successive small gulps.", "reasons": "Muqātil stresses difficulty. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Biqāʿī and others cite bitterness and heat; al-Ṭabrisī adds stench and compulsion. Al-Ṭabarī says thirst makes him swallow despite repulsion. Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as compelled drinking, as reported by al-Wāḥidī. Al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī add thirst and heat; Ibn Kathīr mentions an angel striking with an iron mallet and 22:21. Al-Rāzī stresses continuous gulp by gulp drinking. Al-Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān identify effort or gradual action as possible senses of the form. Ibn ʿAbbās says they dislike the drink, as al-Thaʿlabī reports."}, {"id": "14:17/q02/p2", "position": "The form can equal the simple verb جرع, to gulp.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn list this alongside effort and gradual action; al-Samīn compares ʿadawtu and taʿaddaytuhu. Al-Ālūsī also reports equivalence to the simple verb."}, {"id": "14:17/q02/p3", "position": "The form may express the response or result of making someone gulp.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives it as the result of جرعته; al-Ālūsī reports a passive-response analysis."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q03", "question": "How is يتجرعه connected syntactically to the preceding words?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause describes the water, the drinker while being served, or begins a fresh explanation.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q03/p1", "position": "It modifies the preceding ماء, describing the water.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and Abū al-Baqāʾ as reported by al-Ālūsī allow this adjective analysis."}, {"id": "14:17/q03/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in يسقى.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, Abū al-Baqāʾ and al-Ālūsī allow this analysis."}, {"id": "14:17/q03/p3", "position": "It begins an independent sentence answering an implied question about the drink.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and Abū al-Baqāʾ allow a new sentence. Al-Bursawī supplies the implied question; al-Ālūsī finds this analysis strongest."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q04", "question": "What does يسيغه mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q04/p1", "position": "It means letting the drink pass smoothly down the throat.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Wāḥidī give this sense; al-Wāḥidī cites al-Farrāʾ's poem. Al-Rāzī distinguishes sāgha, passing down, from asāghahu, making it go down. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī include willing acceptance; al-Ālūsī says its negation denies ease and acceptance. Al-Baghawī and Ibn ʿAbbās gloss it as getting it down."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q05", "question": "Does ولا يكاد يسيغه allow the drink to go down?", "turns_on": "How negated kāda works here, and whether other passages and reports require that some liquid actually enter the stomach.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q05/p1", "position": "He cannot swallow it or even nearly do so.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī compare 24:40, where seeing does not occur; al-Baghawī calls kāda an emphatic addition. Al-Zajjāj and Ibn ʿAbbās deny getting the drink down. Al-Zamakhsharī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Nasafī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr say failure to approach swallowing entails failure to swallow; al-Rāzī reports this alternative. Al-Wāḥidī calls the redundant reading less strong; Abū Ḥayyān permits eventual drinking if the cited report is sound. Al-Wāḥidī also points back to his discussion of kāda in 2:20 without restating its analysis."}, {"id": "14:17/q05/p2", "position": "He eventually swallows it, but only after delay and great difficulty.", "reasons": "The idiom mā kidtu aqūmu and 2:71 show eventual action for al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī. Al-Wāḥidī cites 22:20, where the drink melts stomach contents, and repeated sipping as evidence some enters; al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī use the same verse. Al-Baghawī reports that it boils inside him; Abū Ḥayyān makes this conditional on the soundness of the report that he then drinks. Al-Wāḥidī prefers the analysis that keeps kāda meaningful. Ibn Kathīr cites the drink's bad color, taste, smell, and unbearable heat or cold; Study Quran reports choking."}, {"id": "14:17/q05/p3", "position": "He swallows some of the drink but cannot swallow all of it.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbārī's reconciliation, reported by al-Wāḥidī, restricts the negation to the whole drink; al-Rāzī gives the same reconciliation."}, {"id": "14:17/q05/p4", "position": "The denied swallowing is willing acceptance or relish, though liquid may reach his stomach.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says the unbeliever sips in disgust and cannot drink readily in one gulp. Al-Rāzī similarly distinguishes reaching the stomach from true willing swallowing. Al-Ālūsī says sugh includes acceptance."}, {"id": "14:17/q05/p5", "position": "The phrase describes the drinker's attempt to reconcile himself to suffering.", "reasons": "This is Asad's interpretive gloss."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q06", "question": "How are the forms and clauses of يسيغه parsed?", "turns_on": "These are distinct grammatical points about verbal form and circumstantial attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q06/p1", "position": "The verb يسيغه uses the causative form أساغ, which can mean making a drink pass.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the yāʾ has ḍamma because both sāgha al-sharāb and asāghahu ghayruhu occur, the latter being more eloquent."}, {"id": "14:17/q06/p2", "position": "The clause لا يكاد is circumstantial of the drinker, the drink, or both.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī lists all three grammatical attachments."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q07", "question": "What does the report say the drink does to its recipient?", "turns_on": "The extent of the reported effects, especially the extra valley of pus in al-Qummī's version.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q07/p1", "position": "As it nears, it burns his face and scalp; once drunk, it cuts his bowels and exits below.", "reasons": "Abū Umāma transmits the Prophetic account. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Ālūsī and others connect it with 47:15 and 18:29; al-Thaʿlabī also cites 22:20. Al-Ḥākim is said by al-Ālūsī to grade it authentic, and Abū Nuʿaym is said by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī to authenticate it. Some notices stop before the exit detail."}, {"id": "14:17/q07/p2", "position": "One version adds that torn bowels lie beneath his feet and a valley of pus flows

from him.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this expansion from Tafsīr al-Qummī."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q08", "question": "What is meant by الموت coming to the condemned?", "turns_on": "Whether الموت stands for omitted death pangs, for metaphorical deathlike suffering in Hell, or for worldly calamities despite the Hell context.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q08/p1", "position": "The causes, pains, or prolonged agonies of death afflict him without death occurring.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports an ellipsis of agony and distress because actual death cannot arrive while he lives. Al-Ālūsī allows figurative expression or an omitted noun. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī and others describe death's causes and throes; Ibn ʿAbbās says each torment would kill if God allowed it. Al-Qurṭubī reports God creating deathlike pain or prolonging death pangs."}, {"id": "14:17/q08/p2", "position": "Death is a figurative name for deathlike misery and afflictions.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash applies this to Hell's calamities in al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī. Abū Bakr, reported by al-Wāḥidī, calls the breathing sufferer figuratively dead; a report calls poverty the greatest death, and al-Wāḥidī cites a poet contrasting a rested dead person with a miserable living one. Al-Burhān distinguishes figurative death under terror from literal death. Al-Ālūsī reports a specifically worldly-afflictions version."}, {"id": "14:17/q08/p3", "position": "It names severe worldly calamities of disbelievers.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this form of al-Akhfash's reading to him; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī object that the passage describes the Hereafter and Hell."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q09", "question": "What does من كل مكان describe?", "turns_on": "Whether 'place' is a bodily location, an external direction, a kind of lethal ordeal, or an encompassing time and place.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q09/p1", "position": "Pain reaches every part of the body, down to hairs, veins, toes, organs, and joints.", "reasons": "Ibrāhīm al-Taymī repeatedly specifies beneath or to the ends of every hair. Ibn ʿAbbās is also reported for every hair; al-Thawrī specifies every vein; Maymūn names bones, veins, sinews, and nerves; Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb names organs and joints; al-Ḍaḥḥāk adds the big toe. Al-Wāḥidī says most commentators take bodily parts. Al-Ṭabrisī includes inside and outside."}, {"id": "14:17/q09/p2", "position": "Death's causes surround him from every direction, conventionally all six sides.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās lists front, rear, sides, above and below; al-Farrāʾ records four horizontal directions. Al-Qurṭubī cites 39:16's canopies of fire. Al-Damghānī says atā can mean descend. Al-Kashshāf and later sources offer this alongside bodily parts; Abū Ḥayyān calls the six-direction sense apparent."}, {"id": "14:17/q09/p3", "position": "Every kind of torment that could kill him confronts him.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says any one punishment would kill if God so decreed. Al-Qurṭubī specifies bites, stings, fire, chains, and boiling water; al-Nasafī and al-Bursawī similarly say each part of the suffering would be fatal. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb describes successive death experiences on seeing, approaching, and drinking the beverage."}, {"id": "14:17/q09/p4", "position": "The experience pervades every limb, place, and time.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī extends the expression across bodily, spatial, and temporal dimensions."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q10", "question": "Why does he remain not dead amid deathlike suffering?", "turns_on": "The notes either explain the purpose and effect of survival or describe the soul's suspended state.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q10/p1", "position": "He remains alive so he cannot gain the relief of death and his punishment continues.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says he neither dies and rests nor lives with ease. Al-Māwardī and Abū Ḥayyān stress prolonged agony. Al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Qurṭubī cite 35:36; al-Ṭaḥlabī and al-Qurṭubī connect the trapped soul with 20:74, al-Baghawī with 87:13. Ibn Kathīr says this enables perpetual punishment; al-Biqāʿī says God keeps him alive. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb's repeated 'deaths' are experiences short of ending life; al-Qurṭubī rejects literal dying."}, {"id": "14:17/q10/p2", "position": "His soul is held at his throat, unable either to leave or return.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Ibn Jurayj give this mechanism: leaving would bring death, while returning would restore bodily ease or life. Al-Ṭabarī incorporates it in his explanation."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q11", "question": "What does ميت imply about the person's state?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q11/p1", "position": "It describes a present state, while related forms may denote someone who will die.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ contrasts miyyit as an existing condition with māʾit or mayyit for future death, comparing sayyid/sāʾid and karīm/kārim."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q12", "question": "How is ميت read here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q12/p1", "position": "All readers geminate it because death has not yet become an accomplished state.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī notes that contexts where the death has already happened differ."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q13", "question": "What does من ورائه mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the spatial word locates punishment ahead of the person or sequences a further punishment after the present ordeal.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q13/p1", "position": "Ahead of the condemned person, in his still unseen future.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba explains that unseen things can be described as behind or before; al-Ṭabarī cites a poem, a Basran explains the relation to the present, a Kufan says it is especially common of passing times, and another grammarian treats وراء as an antonym. Al-Wāḥidī reports Ibn ʿAbbās placing it before the sinner on Judgment Day. Al-Qurṭubī cites poems and 18:79, and reports explanations based on concealment or pursuit; al-Azharī and Abū ʿUbayda connect both directions to concealment, and Ibn al-Anbārī says Hell is hidden. {"id": "14:17/q19", "question": "How is the cited Banu ʿAjl death poem explained?", "turns_on": "The cited lines shift from the killed man and the revenge taunt to the sword's personified death image.", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q19/p1", "position": "The speaker depicts felling a mighty man and taunts Banu ʿAjl's false claim of blood revenge.", "reasons": "Al-Marzūqī explains that Banu ʿAjl owed revenge to Banu Māzin but killed an uninvolved Yuhsab guest; the poet says the death blow struck the man himself, not his intended target. {"id": "14:17/q21", "question": "How is 'death comes but he is not dead' related to another Qur'anic paradox?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q21/p1", "position": "The apparent contradiction dissolves when each statement is considered in its own respect.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī compares 22:2, 'you see people drunk though they are not': drunkenness is figurative with respect to Judgment's terrors and literal with respect to wine; similarly, deathlike pain comes without literal death."}]}
{"id": "14:17/q22", "question": "What limited relief for other people in Hell is mentioned alongside this punishment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:17/q22/p1", "position": "Reports mention relief for Abū Lahab and Abū Ṭālib; Abū Lahab receives a little water on Mondays.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī says Abū Lahab freed his nurse Thuwayba after she announced Muḥammad's birth; the notice connects this deed to the weekly water and also mentions relief for Abū Ṭālib without giving its details."}]}

{"id": "14:35/q04", "question": "When was this prayer made in relation to the prayer in 2:126?", "turns_on": "Whether the two wordings mark successive occasions, a single retold supplication, or a chronology not fixed by narrative order.", "positions": [{"id": "14:35/q04/p1", "position": "This was a later prayer, after Mecca became a settlement or the House was built.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Rāzī, Biqāʿī, Itqān, Ibn Kathīr, Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Samarrāʾī and Kuran Yolu contrast earlier indefinite baladan with the established al-balad. {"id": "14:35/q21", "question": "What reports describe events linked with the recitation of this prayer?", "turns_on": "The distinct narrated episodes.", "positions": [{"id": "14:35/q21/p1", "position": "The Prophet recited these verses and prayed for his community, receiving good news.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits the report through al-Ṭabarī from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar."}, {"id": "14:35/q21/p2", "position": "At al-ʿAqaba the Prophet recited Abraham's prayer to six Anṣār, who accepted his invitation.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib's account; Ṭabāṭabāʾī repeats it and says the men were moved."}, {"id": "14:35/q21/p3", "position": "The Prophet called himself the answer to Abraham's prayer and foretold his banner of praise.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports his statement that Arabs will be nearest that banner on Judgment Day."}]}
